<reason>PRO opened with a strong, memorable case (timing game, fire engine, "eyes plus hands") but CON progressively narrowed the dispute to what the motion actually asks about: deflection hardware, not telescopes both sides fund. CON's rebuttals landed on the physics PRO itself introduced—asteroids give years, not minutes, so the fire-engine analogy fails; a stored generic impactor still waits for characterization and pre-commits to one method; short windows belong to shelter, which PRO effectively conceded in A4.4. CON's pressure questions were sharper (name the window; what does "budget dust" buy), and PRO's answers—"will likely" land in a middle band, a "handful" of rotating spacecraft—left the hardware's justification looking speculative. PRO's closing concession that the ready fleet "waits for the same tracking data" let CON reduce the hardware's benefit to assembly time at the margin. PRO had a genuinely plausible middle-window argument and better rhetoric, but never squarely answered the characterization-clock point or costed its fleet. CON's clipped turn was a small execution cost only. CON made the decision easier.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.1–B4.3 and B5.2: CON's response that both plans run the same characterization clock, that a generic impactor risks fragmenting a rubble pile, and that PRO's own "rapid reconnaissance and evacuation" line is CON's plan—then exploiting PRO's closing admission that the fleet "waits for the same tracking data" to shrink the hardware's value to assembly time.</best_rebuttal>
